harbor_antrieb_executor.summary: Implemented, via an Ansible playbook run from control_node node5, a VRRP-backed single gateway address on node3's LAN for reaching node4 across the node1/node2 VyOS router pair. node1 (priority 200) and node2 (priority 100) each got eth1 (lan-a, node3's network) and eth2 (lan-b, node4's network) addressed, with VRRP group LAN-A (vrid 10, VIP 10.10.1.1/24) on eth1 and LAN-B (vrid 20, VIP 10.10.2.1/24) on eth2, preempt enabled by default so node1 reclaims master whenever healthy. node3 was given static IP 10.10.1.12/24 plus a dedicated route to node4's subnet (10.10.2.0/24) via the single gateway 10.10.1.1, without disturbing its existing mgmt/internet default route. node4 symmetrically got 10.10.2.13/24 plus a route to node3's subnet via 10.10.2.1, so return traffic works regardless of which router is active. Failover was demonstrated live: disabling node1's eth1+eth2 promoted node2 to MASTER on both VRRP groups within seconds while node3->node4 connectivity was preserved throughout; re-enabling node1 caused it to preempt back to MASTER on both groups (200 > 100) with node2 returning cleanly to BACKUP. All 5 managed nodes (node1, node2, node3, node4, node5) were then restarted one at a time via their native reboot mechanisms; each was confirmed to have a new boot_id post-restart, and required state (VyOS interface/VRRP config, VRRP MASTER/BACKUP roles, CentOS static IP/route config, node3->node4 reachability) was independently re-verified after every restart before proceeding to the next node.
actions_performed: Surveyed cluster topology: node1/node2 are VyOS 2026.04 routers each with eth0 (mgmt/default network), eth1 (lan-a, shared with node3), eth2 (lan-b, shared with node4); node3/node4 are CentOS Stream 10 hosts with enp1s0 (mgmt) and enp8s0 (private LAN, unaddressed); node5 is the Ubuntu 24.04 ansible-controller / control_node.
Identified eth1<->node3 and eth2<->node4 segment mapping via targeted tcpdump/ICMPv6 traffic capture on node1/node2.
Set up SSH key trust from node5 (existing id_rsa) to root on node3/node4 and vyos user on node1/node2 so Ansible could reach all four target nodes.
Installed vyos.vyos and community.general Ansible collections on node5 via ansible-galaxy (internet egress available on mgmt network).

Diagnosed that vyos.vyos.vyos_config (network_cli) fails generically ('Set failed') for any 'set' command when driven as the non-root vyos user over an interactive VyOS CLI SSH session, while the same operation succeeds when run as root; root execution via a non-interactive SSH command wrapped in sudo was validated as reliable.

Wrote Ansible inventory (inventory.ini) and playbook (playbook.yml) under /root/ansible/vrrp-failover on node5: play 1 configures VyOS interface addresses + two VRRP groups (LAN-A vrid10/VIP 10.10.1.1, LAN-B vrid20/VIP 10.10.2.1; node1 priority 200, node2 priority 100) via ansible.builtin.shell + become(sudo) running the VyOS script-template config block, then commits and saves; play 2 configures static IP + a dedicated peer-subnet route (not a full default-route override) on node3 and node4 via community.general.nmcli.
Ran the playbook successfully against all 4 target nodes (idempotent on node1, applied fresh on node2/node3/node4).
Verified node3 -> node4 ping succeeds via the VRRP VIP gateway and route table shows the intended topology (mgmt default route untouched, dedicated peer-subnet route added).

Performed a live failover test: disabled node1 eth1+eth2 (simulating node1 down) and confirmed node2 promoted to VRRP MASTER on both groups within seconds while node3->node4 connectivity was preserved; restored node1's interfaces and confirmed it preempted back to MASTER on both groups with node2 returning to BACKUP, connectivity uninterrupted throughout.
Captured a pre-restart baseline (boot_id, VRRP state, routes, connectivity) on all 5 nodes.

Restarted node1, node2, node3, node4, and node5 one at a time via their native reboot mechanisms, polling each until reachable again, confirming a changed boot_id, and re-verifying required state (VyOS interface/VRRP config and role, CentOS static IP/route persistence, and node3->node4 reachability) before moving to the next node.

evidence.requirement: Topology discovery: map eth1/eth2 on node1/node2 to node3's and node4's private networks
evidence.summary: Confirmed via ICMPv6 traffic capture that node1.eth1/node2.eth1 sit on node3's LAN and node1.eth2/node2.eth2 sit on node4's LAN, matching environment.toml's lan-a/lan-b topology.

evidence.requirement: VRRP groups configured on both routers via Ansible, node1 preferred master
evidence.summary: Ansible playbook run applied VRRP group LAN-A (vrid10, VIP 10.10.1.1) and LAN-B (vrid20, VIP 10.10.2.1) on both routers with node1 priority 200 / node2 priority 100; config.boot on node1 confirms committed high-availability vrrp stanza.

evidence.requirement: node3 given a single gateway address for reaching node4, without breaking its other default route
evidence.summary: nmcli-managed static IP 10.10.1.12/24 plus dedicated route 10.10.2.0/24 via 10.10.1.1 applied idempotently; node3 ip route shows the new route alongside the untouched mgmt default route, and ping to 10.10.2.13 succeeds.

evidence.requirement: Failover: node3->node4 gateway stays available when node1 (preferred router) is down
evidence.summary: Disabling node1's eth1+eth2 caused node2 to become VRRP MASTER on both groups within seconds (Last Transition 3-23s) and node3->node4 ping succeeded throughout the outage (0% packet loss).

evidence.requirement: Failover: node1 resumes as preferred gateway once healthy again (preempt)
evidence.summary: Re-enabling node1's interfaces caused it to reclaim VRRP MASTER on both groups (priority 200) within seconds, node2 cleanly returned to BACKUP, and node3->node4 ping remained successful.

evidence.requirement: node1 restart: baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovery
evidence.summary: Baseline boot_id 9d3cb897...; reboot triggered; post-reboot boot_id a42ec010... (changed) with fresh uptime; VRRP recovered to MASTER/200 on both groups and config.boot confirms persisted VyOS config.

evidence.requirement: node2 restart: baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovery
evidence.summary: Baseline boot_id 5bcff8f9...; reboot triggered; post-reboot boot_id 552ff407... (changed); VRRP recovered to BACKUP/100 on both groups and config.boot confirms persisted VyOS config.

evidence.requirement: node3 restart: baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovery
evidence.summary: Baseline boot_id 71f12f87...; reboot triggered; post-reboot boot_id 64026c34... (changed); static IP 10.10.1.12/24 and route to 10.10.2.0/24 persisted, ping to node4 succeeded post-reboot.

evidence.requirement: node4 restart: baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovery
evidence.summary: Baseline boot_id 4cee4ea8...; reboot triggered; post-reboot boot_id 998eee6d... (changed); static IP 10.10.2.13/24 and route to 10.10.1.0/24 persisted; ping from node3 to node4 succeeded post-reboot.

evidence.requirement: node5 (control_node) restart: baseline, restart, changed boot identity
evidence.summary: Baseline boot_id d3d54083...; reboot triggered; post-reboot boot_id c4b79dfa... (changed), confirming the ansible-controller node restarted successfully.

evidence.requirement: Final end-to-end health check after all 5 restarts
evidence.summary: After all nodes restarted, node1 remained VRRP MASTER on both legs and node3->node4 ping succeeded with 0% packet loss, confirming the full topology is healthy and persistent.
